title: How to get started?
author: OrkWithNoTeef
selftext: I have basic Claude LLM for code, but what do you use to generate assets? And how do you set up for one shots?

comments.author: Ok-Lengthiness-6692
comments.body: What's a one shot? Anyway I use chatgpt to generate assets I like the use adobe fireworks to edit them. What sort of assets you want is entirely subjective to your taste, but you can send the AI examples from other games to get an idea.

comments.author: averageuhbear
comments.body: Learn basic game design and coding without AI first.

comments.author: TyHuffman
comments.body: There are plenty of videos and training materials on YouTube. Jump down that rabbit hole.

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
Truthfully, you just need a game idea in your head, and then you start building. The more detail you have about how the game works, how it looks, how you control the game, the systems, sound, etc., the faster it will go. The current state of AI game dev is not really yet to a “one shot” level. People are running multi agent loops (burning a lot of tokens and technically hundreds / thousands of changes but initiated by the AI agents) set up to do these bigger more complicated projects. 

I think this “one shot“ stuff is very misleading. I’ve been working on a game for a few weeks and I highly doubt you are going to get a real game in one prompt, on your first try. This is like, impossible, if you are just starting out. Also, if you don’t have Claude Pro (US$20/mo) you are not going to have enough tokens to build anything beyond a basic web browser game. 

That being said Claude Code can build some amazing shit seemingly out of thin air if you have a good prompt. As for art, this is a whole different hustle than Claude, there are lots of ways to generate images, but you have to either have some kind of magical perfect asset generator tool (almost never free) or series of prompts that get you to some usable sprites (kind of another smaller “one shot” miracle buy for art) .

Thus, I would recommend that you start building in Godot (free and powerful game engine) use Claude code CLI (command line interface) , set up GitHub and a local folder on your computer, install the Godot MCP (model controller protocol, helps Claude Code speak to the game engine more effectively, and THEN start building. This way, you can get pretty far with vector graphics (line shapes - early arcade stuff but 1000x more intricate, detailed) and/or colored 3D shapes, you can make some pretty compelling game prototypes in the engine with this setup. 

TLDR; one shots are really one shots, have an idea and JUST START

replies.author: OrkWithNoTeef
replies.body: So the videos of claude opus single prompt "make me a racing game"  and it generates and compiles the whole game including all 3d models, textures, assets, sound effects, shaders, physics and so on are fake?

replies.author: ZedIsAPrimeNumber
replies.body: They're mostly real but the games are also just what you see. Games that people really want to play go a lot deeper than that.

replies.author: OrkWithNoTeef
replies.body: Mostly real? What are the parts which aren't?

replies.author: ZedIsAPrimeNumber
replies.body: What's mostly real is that what you see in the demo plays as the demo shows. However, I can guarantee any zero shot prompt doesn't create a fully fleshed out multiplayer mechanics, interesting progression or engaging upgrade paths. They might have those, as in a checked item list "I did it" way, but that's about it.

replies.author: sevenoutdb
replies.body:
okay, I'm going to be honest here, I don't know that there is anyone that is an expert with this stuff since it's changing SO rapidly. Honest request, show me a video where the creator claimed that an LLM one-shots a game and I would be happy to see how they did it and help you do the same. I'm making games but also continuing to learn. I've beem a game producer professionally for decades so I love seeing how people are using this stuff, so that's an honest offer. The most recent "one-shot" examples I've seen are of people prompting Claude, Cursor or Codex to create a multi-agent loop to copy specific existing games, so it's kind of like assigning one agent to research the game they are trying to mimic, get screenshots/footage/info, then another agent to figure out the simplest way to create art for the game, another to start programming, another to test the game, another to tell all the agents what to do next. It's all very much possible, but it takes a lot of trial and error to get these multi-agent setup to make things without falling into investigation traps (it start digging and digging into useless topics), or getting stuck doing really low value work (like spending a signifcant portion of their brain writing a design document, making sparkle effects that you'll only see two times in the game, that kind of stuff) and using a LOT of horsepower/tokens. If you're a creator and you have the $100/mo account and you can just go crazy on this stuff, that different that what you and I are doing, which is using AI as a partner, but not really a whole team of AI agents working together at the same time.

I could be wrong though, like I said, this shit is changing SO fast. 

Whatever you do, START. You don't need permission, you don't need experience, all you need is commitment and desire, the rest will come.

comments.author: rmfrost
comments.body:
One-shots are basically, "create a clone of \[insert game here\]", after which it'll make a "close enough" concept demo, often borrowing from existing open-source versions of that game (if any exist) whenever possible.

AI asset generation is a whole different animal requiring a whole different AI token budget (and likely different AI tools than what you'd intuitively want to use).
